paragraphs.title: Opening of the Prophecy and Presentation of the Parable

easy.explanation: The verse says, “the word of the Lord came unto me,” speaking to Ezekiel.
easy.q: To whom did the word of the Lord come?

easy.explanation: Ezekiel was told to speak the riddle and parable “unto the house of Israel.”
easy.q: To whom was Ezekiel told to speak the riddle and parable?

easy.explanation: He was told to “put forth a riddle, and speak a parable.”
easy.q: What was Ezekiel commanded to present?

answers: The word of the Lord came to him
The vine turned toward the eagle
medium.explanation: First, the word of the Lord came to Ezekiel; then he received the command.
medium.q: What happened before Ezekiel was commanded to speak the parable?

medium.explanation: The command specifically says to speak to the house of Israel.
medium.q: Who was the intended audience of the message?

medium.explanation: A riddle is a puzzling statement whose meaning must be understood.
medium.q: What is a riddle?

answers: It communicates its message through symbolic language
It is addressed only to a king
challenge.explanation: A riddle and parable communicate truth through symbols and figurative meaning.
challenge.q: What does the command to present a riddle and parable indicate about the prophecy?

answers: The parable, the word, and then the command
The word of the Lord, the command, and then the riddle and parable
The exile, the command, and then the word
challenge.explanation: The word comes to Ezekiel, he receives the command, and he is told to present the riddle and parable.
challenge.q: What is the correct sequence in these verses?

answers: Because it is presented as a riddle and parable
Because it is written as a song
challenge.explanation: The form of a riddle and parable signals that the message has a deeper meaning.
challenge.q: Why would the message require interpretation?

paragraphs.title: The First Eagle and the Vine

answers: The highest branch of the cedar
easy.explanation: The eagle “took the highest branch of the cedar.”
easy.q: What did the great eagle take from Lebanon?

easy.explanation: It carried the twigs “into a land of traffick” and set them in a city of merchants.
easy.q: Where did the eagle carry the top of the young twigs?

answers: A spreading vine of low stature
easy.explanation: The seed grew into “a spreading vine of low stature.”
easy.q: What did the planted seed become?

answers: It planted it in a fruitful field by great waters
It carried it back to Lebanon
medium.explanation: The eagle planted the seed in a fruitful field and placed it by great waters.
medium.q: What did the eagle do with the seed of the land?

answers: It was low but brought forth branches and sprigs
It became a mighty cedar immediately
medium.explanation: The vine had low stature, yet it brought forth branches and shot forth sprigs.
medium.q: What characterized the vine as it grew?

answers: The uppermost part of the cedar
medium.explanation: The highest branch is the uppermost part of the tree.
medium.q: What does “the highest branch of the cedar” mean?

answers: They provided favorable conditions for growth
They changed the vine into a cedar
challenge.explanation: The vine was planted by great waters so that it could grow and bear fruit.
challenge.q: How did the waters contribute to the vine’s growth?

answers: A high, prominent tree is contrasted with a low-growing vine
A dry tree is contrasted with a dead branch
A vine is contrasted with a city
challenge.explanation: The eagle takes the high cedar branch, while the planted seed becomes a vine of low stature.
challenge.q: What contrast is shown between the cedar’s branch and the vine?

answers: The vine developed in connection with the place and source from which it came
challenge.explanation: Its growth and direction remained connected with the eagle that planted it.
challenge.q: What does the vine’s branches turning toward the first eagle suggest?

paragraphs.title: The Vine Turns to the Second Eagle

easy.explanation: The vine bent its roots and branches toward another great eagle.
easy.q: Toward whom did the vine bend its roots and shoot forth its branches?

answers: That he might cut down the cedar
That it might escape into the wilderness
easy.explanation: The vine sought water from the second eagle.
easy.q: Why did the vine send its branches toward the second eagle?

answers: It would immediately become a cedar
easy.explanation: The passage repeatedly says that the vine would wither.
easy.q: What would happen to the vine?

medium.explanation: It sent forth its branches so that the second eagle might water it.
medium.q: Why did the vine turn toward the second eagle?

answers: Great waters and growth are contrasted with drying and withering
Egypt is contrasted with Babylon only
A cedar is contrasted with an eagle
medium.explanation: The vine was planted by great waters, but the east wind would cause it to wither.
medium.q: What contrast is made between the vine’s planting and the east wind?

answers: A vine extending outward through its branches
medium.explanation: The phrase describes a vine whose branches spread outward.
medium.q: What does “spreading vine” mean in this passage?

answers: It turns to another source, and the east wind strikes it
challenge.explanation: The vine turns toward another eagle and is ultimately dried by the east wind.
challenge.q: What causes the vine’s failure in the parable?

answers: It seeks water from the second eagle
It bears fruit entirely by itself
challenge.explanation: Its request to be watered shows that the vine depends on an outside source.
challenge.q: Which detail shows that the vine is dependent on another?

answers: Turning toward the second eagle, failure, and withering
Planting, becoming a cedar, and rescue
challenge.explanation: The vine turns toward the second eagle, but the result is failure and withering.
challenge.q: What is the sequence of events described?

paragraphs.title: Interpretation of the Parable: Babylon and Zedekiah’s Covenant

easy.explanation: The interpretation says, “the king of Babylon is come to Jerusalem.”
easy.q: Who came to Jerusalem according to the interpretation?

answers: All the fowls of the air
easy.explanation: He took the king and the princes and led them to Babylon.
easy.q: Whom did the king of Babylon take?

easy.explanation: He made a covenant and oath so that it might be kept.
easy.q: What did the king of Babylon require the king’s seed to keep?

answers: He made a covenant with him and took an oath of him
He made him king over Egypt
He sent him back to Lebanon
medium.explanation: He took the king’s seed, made a covenant with him, and took his oath.
medium.q: What did the king of Babylon do with the king’s seed?

answers: That it should be base and not lift itself up
That it should become independent and powerful
That it should have no ruler
medium.explanation: The kingdom was to be base and remain standing by keeping the covenant.
medium.q: What condition was intended for the kingdom?

medium.explanation: The phrase refers to the influential and powerful people of the land.
medium.q: What does “the mighty of the land” refer to?

answers: Babylon is represented by the first eagle, and the king appointed by Babylon is represented by the planted vine
Egypt is represented by the vine, and the eagle is represented by Zedekiah
The birds represent the kings of Jerusalem
challenge.explanation: The interpretation identifies Babylon with the first eagle and the dependent kingdom with the planted vine.
challenge.q: How does the interpretation correspond to the details of the parable?

answers: So that he would keep the covenant and remain under Babylon’s arrangement
So that he would fight Egypt
So that he would grow a cedar
challenge.explanation: The oath was intended to secure his faithfulness to the covenant.
challenge.q: Why was an oath taken from the king’s seed?

answers: Keeping the covenant would allow the kingdom to stand in a low position
Rebellion would lead to the vine being watered
challenge.explanation: The kingdom could stand by keeping the covenant and not exalting itself.
challenge.q: What cause-and-effect relationship appears in these verses?

easy.explanation: He sent his ambassadors into Egypt.
easy.q: To whom did Zedekiah send his ambassadors?

easy.explanation: He sent to Egypt for horses and much people.
easy.q: What did Zedekiah seek from Egypt?

easy.explanation: The passage says that he broke the covenant.
easy.q: What did Zedekiah do to the covenant?

answers: Egypt would not act with a mighty army and great company to rescue him
medium.explanation: The Lord says Pharaoh would not make for him in the war with sufficient power to save him.
medium.q: Why would Egypt not save Zedekiah?

answers: He would be brought to Babylon and die there
He would be planted on Israel’s mountain
medium.explanation: The king would be brought to Babylon, where he would die.
medium.q: What would happen to the one who broke the covenant?

answers: The people fleeing with or from him
medium.explanation: Fugitives are people who flee or escape.
medium.q: What does “his fugitives” mean?

answers: He despised an oath and broke a covenant
challenge.explanation: The passage emphasizes that he despised the oath and broke the covenant.
challenge.q: What made Zedekiah’s action especially serious?

answers: The consequences would fall upon him personally
He would be appointed as head
challenge.explanation: The phrase means that judgment would come directly upon the offender.
challenge.q: What does “I will recompense upon his own head” mean?

answers: Capture from which there is no escape
challenge.explanation: The Lord spreads a net and takes him in a snare, symbolizing capture.
challenge.q: What does the net symbolize in the judgment?

easy.explanation: The verse says, “shall fall by the sword.”
easy.q: By what would the fugitives fall?

easy.explanation: Those who remained would be scattered toward all winds.
easy.q: Where would those who remained be scattered?

answers: That the vine was a cedar
easy.explanation: The verse ends, “ye shall know that I the Lord have spoken it.”
easy.q: What would the people know as a result?

answers: All the fugitives with all their bands
All the trees of the field
medium.explanation: The verse refers to all the fugitives and their bands.
medium.q: Who would fall by the sword?

medium.explanation: The survivors would no longer remain together but would be dispersed.
medium.q: What does scattering toward all winds signify?

medium.explanation: A fugitive is someone who runs away or escapes.
medium.q: What is a fugitive?

answers: It shows that the announced judgment is fulfilled
It shows that the kingdom becomes stronger
It cancels the word of the Lord
challenge.explanation: The scattering is part of the judgment and confirms the Lord’s declaration.
challenge.q: How does the scattering reinforce the prophetic message?

answers: The fall is a consequence of the rebellion and judgment
The fall results from successful watering
The fall is a sign of a new covenant
challenge.explanation: The scattering follows the rebellion and breach of the covenant.
challenge.q: What is the connection between the fall of the fugitives and the broken covenant?

answers: To emphasize the Lord’s authority and the fulfillment of his word
To identify the place of exile
To explain the shape of the vine
challenge.explanation: The closing statement emphasizes that the events fulfill the Lord’s spoken judgment.
challenge.q: Why does the verse end with “I the Lord have spoken it”?

easy.explanation: The Lord would crop off “a tender one” from the cedar’s young twigs.
easy.q: What would the Lord take from the cedar?

answers: On a high mountain and eminent in Israel
easy.explanation: It would be planted on the high mountain of Israel.
easy.q: Where would the branch be planted?

easy.explanation: The branch would grow and become a goodly cedar.
easy.q: What would the branch become?

answers: Dwell in the shadow of its branches
medium.explanation: All fowl of every wing would dwell in the shadow of its branches.
medium.q: What would the birds do under the cedar?

answers: Planting, bearing boughs and fruit, and becoming a goodly cedar
Drying, being cut down, and then being planted
medium.explanation: The branch is planted, brings forth boughs and fruit, and becomes a goodly cedar.
medium.q: What is the order of development described?

medium.explanation: The phrase describes a mountain that is high and prominent.
medium.q: What does “high mountain and eminent” mean?

answers: The vine is low and dependent, while the new cedar is high and provides shelter
The vine is dry and the cedar is an eagle
Both are described as dry trees
challenge.explanation: The earlier vine is low and dependent, while the new cedar becomes high and sheltering.
challenge.q: What contrast is shown between the earlier vine and the new cedar?

answers: The tree will provide broad shelter and security
The tree will remain very small
The birds will destroy the tree
challenge.explanation: Many birds dwelling beneath it portray the cedar as a wide source of shelter.
challenge.q: What does the presence of every kind of bird under the cedar suggest?

answers: The Lord brings down the high tree, exalts the low tree, dries the green tree, and makes the dry tree flourish
Every tree grows in exactly the same way
challenge.explanation: The verse declares the Lord’s power to reverse the conditions of high, low, green, and dry.
challenge.q: What principle is expressed in the final verse?
